title: Physiology - Cardiovascular (DOMiNANCE Originals)
source: Built from CVS lecture slides (Circulation 1-3, Lectures 5-7)

questions.stem: The structures of the heart responsible for initiating and spreading the heartbeat make up the:
questions.why: The specialised conducting system consists of modified cardiac muscle cells that generate spontaneous impulses and distribute them through the atria and ventricles, coordinating the sequence of contraction.

notes.B: The fibrous skeleton supports the valves and electrically insulates the atria from the ventricles rather than generating the heartbeat.
notes.C: The coronary vascular network supplies oxygen and nutrients to the myocardium, including conducting cells, but does not conduct electrical impulses.
notes.D: The pericardial sac encloses the heart, limits excessive distension and reduces friction as the heart moves.
notes.E: Papillary muscles tense the chordae tendineae during ventricular contraction to prevent atrioventricular valve prolapse, not to initiate impulses.

questions.stem: In the terminology of the cardiac cycle, systole refers to:
questions.why: Systole is the phase of cardiac muscle contraction, during which the affected chamber develops pressure and may eject blood. Diastole is the corresponding relaxation phase.

notes.A: Valve opening depends on pressure differences and occurs during both ventricular ejection and filling, so it does not define systole.
notes.C: Relaxation is diastole, when ventricular pressure falls and eventually permits filling from the atria.
notes.D: Ventricular filling occurs mainly during diastole after ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure, rather than during ventricular systole.
notes.E: Repolarisation restores the electrical membrane potential towards its resting value; it is an electrical event rather than the definition of mechanical contraction.

questions.stem: The resting cardiac output of the right ventricle compared with the left ventricle is:
questions.why: The pulmonary and systemic circulations are connected in series, so the two ventricles must pump approximately equal volumes per minute over time to prevent blood accumulating in either circulation.

notes.A: A persistently greater right ventricular output would deliver blood to the lungs faster than the left ventricle removes it, promoting pulmonary congestion.
notes.B: A persistently smaller right ventricular output would allow blood to accumulate on the systemic venous side and eventually reduce left ventricular filling.
notes.D: If the right ventricle pumped only half the left ventricular output, the imbalance could not persist without redistribution of blood and altered filling.
notes.E: A sustained twofold right ventricular output would overload the pulmonary circulation; the ventricles normally balance their average outputs despite different pressures.

questions.stem: The normal pacemaker of the heart is the:
questions.why: The sinoatrial node has the fastest intrinsic rate of spontaneous diastolic depolarisation among cardiac pacemaker tissues. It normally reaches threshold first and entrains the slower subsidiary pacemakers.

notes.A: The bundle of His conducts impulses across the fibrous cardiac skeleton and can provide a slower escape rhythm if higher pacemakers fail.
notes.B: Purkinje fibres rapidly distribute impulses through ventricular muscle and have slow latent automaticity, normally suppressed by the sinoatrial rhythm.
notes.C: Internodal pathways carry excitation through the atria towards the atrioventricular node; they do not normally determine the heart rate.
notes.E: The atrioventricular junction can generate a slower escape rhythm, typically 40–60 beats per minute, when sinoatrial impulses fail to arrive.

questions.stem: The sinoatrial node is located at the junction of the right atrium and the:
questions.why: The sinoatrial node lies subepicardially near the junction of the superior vena cava and right atrium, at the superior end of the sulcus terminalis.

notes.A: The inferior vena cava enters the lower right atrium; the sinoatrial node lies superiorly near the other caval opening.
notes.B: The coronary sinus opens into the inferior right atrium near the triangle of Koch, a landmark for the atrioventricular node.
notes.C: The pulmonary trunk arises from the right ventricle and carries blood to the lungs rather than joining the right atrium.
notes.D: The tricuspid valve guards the right atrioventricular opening; the sinoatrial node is situated higher in the right atrial wall.

questions.stem: The atrioventricular node is situated in the:

options.label: D
options.text: wall of the superior vena cava

questions.why: The atrioventricular node lies in the inferior interatrial septal region, within the triangle of Koch near the coronary sinus ostium and septal tricuspid annulus. It delays atrial impulses before ventricular activation.

notes.B: The anterior left atrial wall contains working atrial myocardium; the atrioventricular node is approached from the right atrial septal side.
notes.C: The left ventricular apex receives excitation through the distal Purkinje network and is far from the atrioventricular nodal region.
notes.D: The superior vena caval junction is a landmark for the sinoatrial node, not the more inferior atrioventricular node.
notes.E: The ventricular septal apex contains distal conduction fibres, whereas the atrioventricular node lies above the ventricular septum near the tricuspid annulus.

questions.stem: Which is the correct sequence of impulse conduction through the heart?

options.label: A
options.text: AV node, His, SA node, Purkinje fibres

options.label: B
options.text: SA node, AV node, bundle of His, Purkinje fibres

options.label: C
options.text: AV node, SA node, Purkinje fibres, His

options.label: D
options.text: SA node, His, AV node, Purkinje fibres

options.label: E
options.text: Purkinje fibres, His, AV node, SA node

questions.why: Excitation originates in the sinoatrial node, spreads through atrial myocardium and reaches the atrioventricular node. After nodal delay, the His bundle and bundle branches deliver it to the Purkinje network.

notes.A: This sequence starts in the atrioventricular node and places the sinoatrial node downstream of His, reversing the normal atrial initiation pathway.
notes.C: Normal excitation starts in the sinoatrial node, and the His bundle must activate before its distal Purkinje network.
notes.D: The atrioventricular node normally delays the impulse before it reaches the His bundle, not after transmission into the bundle.
notes.E: This sequence describes conduction in reverse; Purkinje fibres normally receive impulses from the bundle branches rather than initiating each heartbeat.

questions.stem: The anterior internodal tract connecting the atria to the AV node is also known as the tract of:
questions.why: In the classical description of atrial conduction, the anterior internodal pathway is associated with Bachmann, with an interatrial branch carrying excitation to the left atrium. Modern anatomy emphasises preferential conduction through atrial muscle.

notes.A: Purkinje fibres form the terminal ventricular conducting network and are not an anterior atrial internodal pathway.
notes.B: The bundle of His connects the atrioventricular node to the ventricular bundle branches rather than linking the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes.
notes.D: Wenckebach is associated with the middle internodal pathway in the classical description, not the anterior pathway.
notes.E: Thorel is associated with the posterior internodal pathway in the classical description, rather than the anterior route.

questions.stem: During normal diastole, the state of the heart valves is that the:

options.label: C
options.text: mitral and aortic valves are open

options.label: D
options.text: mitral and tricuspid valves are open

options.label: E
options.text: aortic and pulmonary valves are open

questions.why: In diastole the AV (mitral and tricuspid) valves are open and the semilunar valves closed, allowing filling.

questions.stem: What proportion of ventricular filling normally occurs passively, before atrial contraction?
questions.why: Most ventricular filling occurs passively after atrioventricular valves open, driven by the atrioventricular pressure gradient. In the lecture convention, about 70% is passive and atrial contraction contributes the remaining 30%.

notes.A: About 30% is the active atrial contribution in the stated teaching convention, not the predominant passive component.
notes.B: Half of filling would overestimate the usual dependence on atrial contraction in a healthy resting heart.
notes.C: Ten per cent substantially underestimates the passive filling that occurs before atrial contraction in normal resting physiology.
notes.D: Passive filling can vary with heart rate and compliance, but 90% exceeds the usual approximate teaching value of 70–80%.

questions.stem: The phase in which the ventricle contracts with all valves closed and no change in volume is:
questions.why: During isovolumetric contraction, ventricular pressure rises after atrioventricular valve closure but before semilunar valve opening. With no inlet or outlet open, ventricular volume remains constant at end-diastolic volume.

notes.B: Rapid ejection begins when ventricular pressure exceeds arterial pressure and opens the semilunar valves, allowing ventricular volume to fall.
notes.C: Isovolumetric relaxation also occurs with all valves closed, but ventricular pressure falls rather than rising as the myocardium relaxes.
notes.D: Rapid filling follows atrioventricular valve opening and increases ventricular volume as blood enters from the atria.
notes.E: Atrial systole increases ventricular filling through open atrioventricular valves, rather than raising ventricular pressure at constant volume.

questions.stem: The left ventricular pressure must exceed roughly what value before the aortic valve opens?
questions.why: The aortic valve opens when left ventricular pressure exceeds the pressure in the aortic root, which at end-diastole is approximately 80 mmHg in a normotensive adult.

notes.A: Around 25 mmHg is closer to normal peak right ventricular systolic pressure, far below the usual aortic opening pressure.
notes.C: Around 10 mmHg may approximate left ventricular end-diastolic pressure but is insufficient to overcome normal aortic diastolic pressure.
notes.D: About 120 mmHg is typical peak left ventricular systolic pressure reached during ejection, after the aortic valve has opened.
notes.E: A pressure of 40 mmHg remains below typical aortic diastolic pressure, so the valve would normally remain closed.

questions.stem: The end-diastolic ventricular volume is approximately:
questions.why: End-diastolic volume is the amount of blood in a ventricle immediately before systole, after passive filling and atrial contraction. A typical teaching value is about 120–130 mL.

notes.A: A volume of 200 mL exceeds the usual resting end-diastolic volume and may occur with marked ventricular dilatation or increased filling.
notes.B: A volume of 90 mL is lower than the standard resting end-diastolic teaching value and closer to a large resting stroke volume.
notes.D: Approximately 70 mL is a typical resting stroke volume, the amount expelled rather than the total volume before contraction.
notes.E: Approximately 50 mL is a typical end-systolic residual volume left in the ventricle after ejection, not the filled volume.

questions.stem: The stroke volume, the amount ejected per beat, is normally about:
questions.why: Stroke volume equals end-diastolic volume minus end-systolic volume. A ventricle containing about 130 mL before contraction and 50 mL afterwards ejects approximately 80 mL per beat.

notes.A: A volume of 130–150 mL is closer to normal end-diastolic volume, not the amount normally ejected at rest.
notes.B: A volume of 40–50 mL is closer to a typical end-systolic volume and would represent a relatively low resting stroke volume.
notes.C: A stroke volume of 100–120 mL can occur with increased filling or exercise but exceeds the usual resting teaching range.
notes.E: A stroke volume of 10–20 mL would be markedly reduced for an adult and is not typical of normal resting cardiac function.

questions.stem: The ejection fraction of a normal ventricle is approximately:
questions.why: Ejection fraction is stroke volume divided by end-diastolic volume, expressed as a percentage. A ventricle ejecting around 80 mL from 125 mL has an ejection fraction of approximately 64%.

notes.A: An ejection fraction of 100% would require complete ventricular emptying, whereas a normal ventricle retains blood after systole.
notes.B: An ejection fraction around 40% indicates reduced left ventricular systolic function rather than normal resting emptying.
notes.C: An ejection fraction of 85% exceeds the usual normal resting range and may reflect a small hyperdynamic ventricle.
notes.D: An ejection fraction of 25% indicates severely reduced systolic emptying, not the normal proportion of end-diastolic blood ejected.

questions.stem: The brief interval after full contraction, during which ventricular pressure begins to fall and ends with closure of the semilunar valves, is called:
questions.why: Protodiastole is the brief transitional period at the end of ventricular ejection when ventricular pressure falls and forward flow decelerates. Semilunar valve closure marks its end.

notes.B: Isovolumetric relaxation begins after semilunar valve closure, so it follows rather than describes the protodiastolic interval.
notes.C: Rapid ejection occurs earlier in systole, when ventricular contraction drives brisk blood flow through open semilunar valves.
notes.D: Reduced filling occurs later in diastole, after atrioventricular valves open and the initial rapid filling phase slows.
notes.E: Atrial systole occurs near the end of ventricular diastole and augments filling before the next ventricular contraction.

questions.stem: According to Starling's law of the heart, the force of contraction is proportional to the:

options.label: B
options.text: initial length of the muscle fibre

options.label: D
options.text: prevailing heart rate at the time

questions.why: The Frank–Starling mechanism increases the force developed by cardiac muscle when its initial fibre length increases within the physiological range. Greater filling therefore normally increases stroke volume without increased intrinsic contractility.

notes.A: Ventricular wall thickness influences wall stress and pressure-generating capacity, but it is not the length-dependent variable in the Frank–Starling relationship.
notes.C: Afterload opposes ventricular ejection and can alter stroke volume, but the Frank–Starling law specifically concerns initial myocardial fibre length.
notes.D: Heart rate affects filling time and cardiac output; the Frank–Starling mechanism links contraction strength to initial stretch rather than pacing rate.
notes.E: Adrenaline increases contractility at a given fibre length through adrenergic signalling, which is distinct from length-dependent Frank–Starling regulation.

questions.stem: Preload is best defined as the:

options.label: C
options.text: degree of myocardial stretch before contraction

options.label: D
options.text: resistance against which blood is expelled

questions.why: Preload describes myocardial fibre stretch immediately before contraction, commonly approximated clinically by ventricular end-diastolic volume or pressure. Increased preload normally increases contraction force through the Frank–Starling mechanism.

notes.A: The rate of ventricular relaxation is a lusitropic property that influences filling but does not itself define the initial fibre stretch.
notes.B: The volume ejected per beat is stroke volume, which is an outcome affected by preload, afterload and contractility.
notes.D: Resistance opposing ventricular ejection describes afterload, a mechanical load during contraction rather than stretch before contraction.
notes.E: The force developed during contraction depends partly on preload and intrinsic contractility, but preload refers to the preceding stretch.

questions.stem: Afterload on the left ventricle corresponds most closely to the:

options.label: A
options.text: the venous return reaching the heart

options.label: B
options.text: the intrinsic rate of the pacemaker

options.label: E
options.text: the degree of diastolic stretch applied

questions.why: Left ventricular afterload is the load opposing myocardial shortening during ejection. It depends largely on aortic pressure and ventricular wall stress, with arterial resistance and compliance influencing that pressure.

notes.A: Venous return supplies ventricular filling and therefore influences preload, rather than directly defining the load opposing left ventricular ejection.
notes.B: The intrinsic pacemaker rate determines the frequency of spontaneous cardiac excitation, not the mechanical load against which the ventricle contracts.
notes.C: End-diastolic muscle fibre length represents initial myocardial stretch and is related to preload rather than afterload.
notes.E: Diastolic stretch describes preload established before ventricular contraction, not the arterial load opposing blood ejection.

questions.stem: Regulation of cardiac output by changes in muscle fibre length is termed:
questions.why: Heterometric regulation adjusts contraction force through changes in initial myocardial fibre length, as in the Frank–Starling mechanism. Homometric regulation changes contractility without requiring an increase in fibre length.

notes.A: Homometric regulation changes force at a given initial fibre length, rather than using altered filling and fibre stretch.
notes.B: Chronotropic regulation alters heart rate and can influence cardiac output, but does not specifically describe length-dependent changes in force.
notes.C: Autoregulation is a broader term for intrinsic regulation and does not identify the specific length-dependent mechanism requested.
notes.D: Neural regulation uses autonomic input to alter cardiac performance, whereas heterometric regulation is an intrinsic response to initial fibre stretch.

questions.stem: A change in the strength of cardiac contraction, independent of fibre length, is called a(n):
questions.why: An inotropic effect changes intrinsic myocardial contractility at a given initial fibre length and loading condition. Positive inotropy increases force development, as occurs with sympathetic stimulation.

notes.B: A chronotropic effect changes the rate of cardiac impulse generation rather than directly describing myocardial contractile strength.
notes.C: A dromotropic effect changes conduction velocity, especially through the atrioventricular node, rather than the force of contraction.
notes.D: A bathmotropic effect changes myocardial excitability or the ease with which an action potential is triggered, not intrinsic contractile strength.
notes.E: A lusitropic effect changes myocardial relaxation, influencing diastolic filling rather than defining systolic contractile force.

questions.stem: Catecholamines increase myocardial contractility mainly by acting on which receptors?
questions.why: Cardiac beta-1 adrenergic receptors activate Gs proteins, adenylyl cyclase and the cAMP–protein kinase A pathway. Increased calcium entry and sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium release strengthen contraction.

notes.A: Nicotinic receptors mediate cholinergic transmission in autonomic ganglia but are not the main myocardial receptors for catecholamine-induced inotropy.
notes.C: Alpha-1 receptors mainly mediate vascular smooth muscle contraction, although cardiac alpha-1 signalling can contribute to inotropy in some circumstances.
notes.D: Cardiac muscarinic M2 receptors mediate parasympathetic signalling and tend to reduce cAMP and nodal activity rather than mediate sympathetic positive inotropy.
notes.E: Beta-2 receptors can contribute to cardiac responses and mediate smooth muscle relaxation, but beta-1 receptors predominate in the normal myocardial response.

questions.stem: Caffeine and theophylline increase cardiac contractility because they:
questions.why: Methylxanthines such as theophylline can inhibit phosphodiesterases, decreasing cAMP breakdown and enhancing calcium-dependent contractility. Adenosine receptor antagonism also contributes to methylxanthine cardiac effects, particularly at lower concentrations.

notes.A: Reducing calcium entry generally weakens cardiac contraction because less trigger calcium is available for sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium release.
notes.B: Depleting catecholamines would reduce adrenergic stimulation rather than explain the positive inotropic effect of methylxanthines.
notes.D: Blocking beta-1 receptors reduces adrenergic cAMP production and generally decreases contractility rather than producing the stated positive inotropic response.
notes.E: Vagal stimulation predominantly slows nodal activity and can reduce atrial contractility, rather than explaining methylxanthine-induced increases in contraction force.

questions.stem: It is impossible to tetanise cardiac muscle because of its:
questions.why: The prolonged cardiac action potential, particularly its calcium-dependent plateau, produces a refractory period that overlaps most of the contraction. A second effective excitation cannot arrive early enough for sustained tetanic summation.

notes.A: Cardiac muscle receives autonomic innervation, although its intrinsic pacemaker activity does not depend on nerves; innervation does not explain the absence of tetany.
notes.B: Abundant mitochondria provide ATP for continuous aerobic cardiac work, but do not determine the electrical refractory period preventing tetanic summation.
notes.C: Calcium entry during the plateau contributes to contraction and action potential duration, but a continuous pathological calcium leak is not the normal anti-tetany mechanism.
notes.E: Cardiomyocytes are relatively small branched cells, but cell size does not prevent repeated excitation during a prolonged refractory period.

questions.stem: On the electrocardiogram, the P wave represents:
questions.why: The P wave records the summed electrical activity of atrial depolarisation as excitation spreads from the sinoatrial region through both atria. Atrial mechanical contraction follows this electrical event.

notes.A: Ventricular depolarisation generates the QRS complex because the large ventricular muscle mass produces a prominent electrical deflection.
notes.B: Ventricular repolarisation generates the T wave, which occurs after ventricular depolarisation rather than before ventricular activation.
notes.C: Atrial repolarisation usually overlaps the QRS complex and is obscured by the much larger ventricular electrical signal.
notes.D: The ventricular action potential plateau corresponds broadly to the ST segment, when most ventricular muscle remains depolarised.

questions.stem: The QRS complex of the ECG represents:
questions.why: The QRS complex represents the spread of depolarisation through the ventricles via the His–Purkinje system and ventricular myocardium. Its electrical activation precedes the development of ventricular contraction.

notes.B: Atrial depolarisation produces the P wave before ventricular activation, rather than the larger QRS deflection.
notes.C: Ventricular repolarisation produces the T wave as ventricular muscle returns towards its resting electrical state.
notes.D: Atrial repolarisation is usually concealed within the QRS complex but is not the principal electrical event generating that complex.
notes.E: Atrioventricular nodal delay contributes to the PR interval and segment before ventricular depolarisation begins.

questions.stem: The normal PR interval ranges from:
questions.why: The PR interval extends from the onset of the P wave to the onset of the QRS complex. Normally 0.12–0.20 seconds, it includes atrial conduction and atrioventricular conduction delay.

notes.A: A PR interval of 0.40–0.60 seconds would be markedly prolonged and could indicate severe atrioventricular conduction delay.
notes.C: A PR interval of 0.06–0.10 seconds is abnormally short for an adult and may suggest pre-excitation or an abnormal atrial origin.
notes.D: Values above 0.20 seconds represent prolonged atrioventricular conduction; the proposed range extends well beyond the normal upper limit.
notes.E: An interval of 0.02–0.08 seconds is too short to account for normal atrial activation and atrioventricular conduction delay.

questions.stem: The T wave of the electrocardiogram corresponds to:
questions.why: The T wave reflects ventricular repolarisation, as ventricular myocytes restore their resting membrane potential after the action potential plateau. Its direction depends on the sequence of repolarisation.

notes.A: Atrial depolarisation produces the P wave before the QRS complex, not the later T wave.
notes.B: Atrioventricular conduction is reflected mainly in the PR interval between atrial and ventricular activation, not the T wave.
notes.D: Ventricular depolarisation produces the QRS complex, preceding the ST segment and subsequent ventricular repolarisation.
notes.E: Atrial repolarisation is usually hidden by the QRS complex and does not generate the normal T wave.

questions.stem: ST-segment depression or elevation is important in the diagnosis of:
questions.why: Myocardial ischaemia alters ventricular action potentials and creates regional electrical potential differences that may shift the ST segment. ST elevation or depression can support an ischaemic diagnosis when interpreted with symptoms and other ECG findings.

notes.A: First-degree atrioventricular block is identified by a prolonged PR interval, not primarily by ST-segment displacement.
notes.B: Bundle branch block primarily widens and changes QRS morphology; secondary ST-T changes may occur but are not its defining finding.
notes.C: Sinus arrhythmia changes successive RR intervals with preserved sinus activation rather than primarily shifting the ST segment.
notes.E: Atrial enlargement alters P-wave amplitude or duration, whereas ischaemic ST changes reflect altered ventricular electrical behaviour.

questions.stem: On standard ECG paper, one small (1 mm) square represents how much time?
questions.why: At the standard ECG recording speed of 25 mm per second, each 1 mm horizontal division represents 1/25 second, or 0.04 seconds. Five small squares equal 0.20 seconds.

notes.A: At 25 mm per second, 0.10 seconds spans 2.5 small horizontal squares rather than a single division.
notes.B: A duration of 0.20 seconds corresponds to one large 5 mm square at standard recording speed, not one small square.
notes.C: A single small square represents 0.02 seconds at 50 mm per second, not at the specified standard speed.
notes.D: A duration of 0.01 seconds would require 100 mm per second for each millimetre, rather than standard ECG paper speed.

questions.stem: Heart rate can be estimated by dividing which number by the number of large squares between two R waves?
questions.why: At the standard ECG paper speed of 25 mm/s, each large square represents 0.20 seconds. There are 300 large squares per minute, so dividing 300 by the RR interval in large squares estimates a regular heart rate.

notes.B: The value 1500 is used when the RR interval is measured in small squares, each representing 0.04 seconds.
notes.C: The value 60 is divided by the RR interval measured in seconds, not by the number of large squares.
notes.D: There are 300 large squares per minute at standard recording speed, so using 100 would underestimate the rate threefold.
notes.E: The value 25 represents the paper speed in millimetres per second, not the number of large squares per minute.

questions.stem: The first heart sound is produced by closure of the:
questions.why: The first heart sound arises from vibrations of the atrioventricular valve apparatus, surrounding myocardium and blood as rising ventricular pressure closes the mitral and tricuspid valves at the onset of systole.

notes.A: Mitral closure contributes the usually louder M1 component, but tricuspid closure also contributes to the first heart sound.
notes.C: Aortic and pulmonary valve closure generates the second heart sound at the end of ventricular ejection, rather than the first.
notes.D: Mitral closure contributes to the first sound, whereas aortic closure contributes to the second sound later in the cardiac cycle.
notes.E: Tricuspid closure contributes to the first sound, but pulmonary closure occurs near the end of systole and contributes to the second.

questions.stem: The second heart sound marks the:
questions.why: The second heart sound is generated by closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves when ventricular pressure falls below arterial pressure. It marks the transition from ventricular ejection to isovolumetric relaxation.

notes.A: Rapid ventricular filling starts after atrioventricular valve opening, which follows the second heart sound and isovolumetric relaxation.
notes.B: Isovolumetric contraction starts after atrioventricular valve closure, which produces the first rather than the second heart sound.
notes.D: The beginning of ventricular systole is associated with the first heart sound and the subsequent rise in ventricular pressure.
notes.E: Atrial contraction occurs late in ventricular diastole and may generate a fourth sound in the presence of reduced ventricular compliance.

questions.stem: Physiological splitting of the second heart sound during inspiration occurs because the:

options.label: C
options.text: aortic and pulmonary valves close together

options.label: D
options.text: aortic valve closes before the pulmonary valve

options.label: E
options.text: pulmonary valve closes before the aortic valve

questions.why: Inspiration increases systemic venous return, prolonging right ventricular ejection and delaying pulmonary valve closure. Aortic closure normally precedes pulmonary closure, and the interval between them widens during inspiration.

notes.A: Mitral closure contributes to the first heart sound; its timing does not explain physiological splitting of the second sound.
notes.B: Tricuspid closure forms part of the first sound, whereas inspiratory splitting concerns the timing of the two semilunar valves.
notes.C: Simultaneous semilunar valve closure would produce no audible splitting, rather than the wider separation normally heard during inspiration.
notes.E: Pulmonary closure preceding aortic closure produces reversed or paradoxical splitting, rather than the usual inspiratory sequence of the second sound.

questions.stem: A third heart sound in diastole, when present, is due to:

options.label: B
options.text: atrial contraction against a closed valve

options.label: C
options.text: turbulent flow across a stenosed valve

questions.why: The third heart sound occurs in early diastole during rapid passive ventricular filling, when deceleration of incoming blood and vibration of the ventricular structures produce a low-frequency sound. It can be physiological in young people.

notes.A: Aortic closure produces the aortic component of the second heart sound, before rapid ventricular filling begins.
notes.B: Atrial contraction occurs near the end of diastole and may generate a fourth sound against a stiff ventricle with an open atrioventricular valve.
notes.C: Flow across a stenosed valve can generate a murmur, which is a more prolonged sound than the early diastolic third sound.
notes.D: During isovolumetric relaxation all valves are closed and ventricular volume remains constant, so the rapid inflow responsible for S3 has not begun.

questions.stem: A heart murmur is generally caused by:
questions.why: A murmur is a prolonged audible vibration associated with disturbed blood flow. High velocity through a narrowed valve, regurgitation through an incompetent valve or increased flow through a normal valve can generate turbulence.

notes.B: Laminar flow is orderly and generally produces little audible vibration, unlike the disturbed flow associated with murmurs.
notes.C: Normal valve closure produces the brief first and second heart sounds, not a sustained flow-related murmur.
notes.D: A slow heart rate alters the intervals between heart sounds but does not by itself create the disturbed blood flow responsible for murmurs.
notes.E: Reduced circulating volume generally lowers filling and flow; it is not the direct mechanism generating a flow-related murmur.

questions.stem: The arterial pulse that can be palpated is produced by:

options.label: B
options.text: a pressure wave expanding the arterial wall

options.label: C
options.text: the actual velocity of the blood column

questions.why: Ventricular ejection creates a pressure disturbance that propagates through the arterial tree and transiently distends its walls. This travelling pressure wave, rather than the movement of an individual parcel of blood, is palpated as the pulse.

notes.A: Arterial smooth muscle regulates vessel diameter and tone but does not actively contract in sequence to generate each palpable arterial pulse.
notes.C: Blood velocity describes the movement of blood itself and is distinct from the much faster propagation of the arterial pressure wave.
notes.D: Aortic closure contributes to the dicrotic notch of the arterial pressure waveform, whereas the main pulse upstroke originates during ventricular ejection.
notes.E: Turbulence can produce an audible bruit or palpable thrill, but a normal arterial pulse does not require turbulent blood flow.

questions.stem: As a person ages, the arterial pulse wave travels:

options.label: A
options.text: faster, because the heart rate rises

options.label: B
options.text: slower, because blood becomes more viscous

options.label: C
options.text: faster, because arteries become more rigid

options.label: D
options.text: slower, because arteries become more elastic

questions.why: Ageing commonly increases arterial stiffness through structural changes in elastin and collagen. Lower arterial compliance increases pulse-wave velocity, so the pressure disturbance reaches peripheral sites more rapidly.

notes.A: Heart rate determines the frequency of pressure pulses, not the principal mechanical determinant of their propagation speed through arteries.
notes.B: Blood viscosity influences resistance to flow, but age-related arterial stiffening is the main explanation for increased pulse-wave velocity.
notes.D: Greater arterial compliance would generally slow pressure-wave propagation, whereas ageing commonly reduces rather than increases compliance.
notes.E: Pulse-wave velocity typically increases as arterial walls become stiffer, although the magnitude varies with blood pressure and vascular health.

questions.stem: The 'a' wave of the jugular venous pulse is produced by:
questions.why: The jugular venous pulse reflects pressure changes in the right atrium. Right atrial contraction transiently raises atrial pressure near the end of ventricular diastole, generating the a wave transmitted into the jugular veins.

notes.A: Tricuspid opening allows blood to drain rapidly into the right ventricle, producing the y descent rather than the a wave.
notes.B: Passive right atrial filling against a closed tricuspid valve produces the v wave during ventricular systole.
notes.C: Ventricular ejection follows atrial contraction and is associated with the systolic portion of the jugular waveform, not the atrial contraction wave.
notes.E: Atrial relaxation contributes to the x descent by reducing right atrial pressure after contraction, rather than producing the a wave.

questions.stem: A giant 'a' wave in the jugular venous pulse is characteristically seen in:
questions.why: In heart block the atrium contracts against a closed tricuspid valve, producing a giant 'a' wave.

questions.stem: Cardiac output is correctly expressed as:
questions.why: Cardiac output is the volume pumped by one ventricle per minute. Multiplying heart rate in beats per minute by stroke volume in millilitres per beat gives output in millilitres per minute.

notes.B: Dividing stroke volume by heart rate does not yield volume per minute and incorrectly predicts lower output when rate increases at fixed stroke volume.
notes.C: Ejection fraction is the proportion of end-diastolic volume expelled, so multiplying it by heart rate omits the absolute volume ejected.
notes.D: Multiplying stroke volume by ejection fraction gives a volume-related quantity but omits the number of beats occurring per minute.
notes.E: Pulse pressure is the difference between systolic and diastolic arterial pressures; multiplying it by heart rate does not calculate blood flow.

questions.stem: The cardiac index is the cardiac output expressed per unit of:
questions.why: Cardiac index normalises cardiac output to body surface area, allowing comparison between individuals of different body sizes. It is expressed in litres per minute per square metre rather than litres per minute alone.

notes.A: Ventricular volume is used when calculating indices of ventricular filling or ejection, not the standard denominator of cardiac index.
notes.C: Body weight can be used to express weight-normalised blood flow, especially in children, but standard cardiac index uses body surface area.
notes.D: Heart mass is relevant to myocardial workload or perfusion per unit tissue, not the conventional body-size adjustment of cardiac output.
notes.E: Dividing output by blood volume relates flow to circulating volume and does not produce the standard body-surface-area-normalised cardiac index.

questions.stem: Vagal (parasympathetic) stimulation of the heart produces a:
questions.why: Vagal acetylcholine activates cardiac M2 muscarinic receptors, decreasing cAMP and increasing potassium conductance in pacemaker cells. Slower spontaneous depolarisation delays threshold attainment and reduces sinoatrial firing frequency, producing negative chronotropy.

notes.A: Parasympathetic stimulation tends to reduce atrial contractility and has relatively limited direct ventricular effects, rather than increasing myocardial force.
notes.B: Vagal stimulation slows atrioventricular nodal conduction through muscarinic signalling, producing negative rather than positive dromotropy.
notes.D: Positive inotropy means increased contractile strength and is more characteristic of sympathetic beta-1 receptor stimulation than vagal stimulation.
notes.E: Positive chronotropy means an increase in heart rate, whereas vagal activity slows spontaneous firing of the sinoatrial node.

questions.stem: Which of the following would INCREASE end-diastolic volume (and thus stroke volume by Starling's law)?
questions.why: Increased venous tone reduces venous capacitance and mobilises blood from the peripheral reservoir, raising the pressure driving venous return. Greater ventricular filling normally increases end-diastolic volume and stroke volume through the Frank–Starling mechanism.

notes.A: A haemodynamically significant pericardial effusion compresses the heart and restricts diastolic filling rather than increasing end-diastolic volume.
notes.B: Increased ventricular stiffness reduces compliance, so a given filling pressure produces less ventricular expansion rather than greater end-diastolic volume.
notes.C: Raised intrapericardial pressure opposes ventricular distension by reducing transmural filling pressure and can therefore decrease ventricular filling.
notes.E: Standing causes gravitational pooling of blood below the heart, initially reducing central venous return and ventricular end-diastolic volume.

questions.stem: Which factor would DECREASE end-diastolic volume?
questions.why: On standing, gravity increases hydrostatic pressure in dependent veins and promotes blood pooling in the lower body. The transient reduction in central blood volume decreases venous return and ventricular end-diastolic volume.

notes.A: Stronger atrial contraction can increase the final contribution to ventricular filling, provided atrioventricular valves are open and ventricular compliance permits filling.
notes.B: Increased circulating blood volume generally raises mean systemic filling pressure and promotes venous return, rather than reducing ventricular filling.
notes.C: Skeletal muscle contraction compresses veins, and one-way valves direct displaced blood towards the heart, supporting ventricular filling.
notes.D: A greater pressure gradient driving venous return or atrioventricular inflow generally promotes filling when resistance and other conditions remain unchanged.

questions.stem: During exercise, cardiac output rises partly because afterload falls as a result of:
questions.why: Exercise causes vasodilatation in active muscle, lowering peripheral resistance and afterload.

questions.stem: Which of the following depresses myocardial contractility?
questions.why: Acidosis depresses myocardial contractility partly by reducing myofilament sensitivity to calcium and disturbing calcium handling. Consequently, a given intracellular calcium transient generates less force, particularly during severe metabolic or respiratory acidosis.

notes.A: Theophylline can inhibit phosphodiesterase and antagonise adenosine receptors, producing cardiac stimulation rather than the typical negative inotropic effect of acidosis.
notes.C: Adrenaline stimulates cardiac beta-1 receptors, increasing cAMP-dependent calcium handling and generally enhancing myocardial contractile strength.
notes.D: Sympathetic stimulation increases calcium entry and release through beta-adrenergic signalling, normally producing a positive inotropic effect.
notes.E: Caffeine is a methylxanthine that can promote cardiac stimulation through adenosine antagonism and concentration-dependent effects on calcium and cAMP signalling.

questions.stem: The Fick principle measures cardiac output using oxygen as the indicator; output equals oxygen consumption divided by the:
questions.why: The Fick principle equates whole-body oxygen consumption with blood flow multiplied by the difference between arterial and mixed venous oxygen content. Rearranging gives cardiac output as oxygen consumption divided by that arteriovenous oxygen difference.

notes.A: Total blood volume measures the amount of circulating blood, but it does not quantify oxygen removed from each unit of blood.
notes.B: Pulmonary artery pressure describes haemodynamic pressure, not the amount of oxygen extracted from blood as it passes through systemic tissues.
notes.D: Arterial oxygen content measures oxygen delivered per unit blood but ignores the oxygen remaining in venous blood after tissue extraction.
notes.E: Mixed venous oxygen content measures residual oxygen after systemic extraction; the calculation requires subtracting it from arterial oxygen content.

questions.stem: For the Fick principle applied to the whole body, the true mixed venous oxygen sample is taken from the:
questions.why: The pulmonary artery receives blood from the right ventricle after systemic venous and coronary venous streams have mixed. Its oxygen content therefore provides the standard mixed venous measurement for whole-body Fick cardiac output.

notes.A: Femoral venous blood reflects oxygen extraction from the drained lower limb and is not representative of all systemic venous territories.
notes.B: Right atrial blood may contain incompletely mixed caval and coronary sinus streams, making pulmonary arterial sampling preferable for true mixed venous content.
notes.C: The coronary sinus drains much of the myocardium and contains particularly oxygen-depleted blood, not the pooled venous return from the whole body.
notes.E: Aortic blood represents systemic arterial oxygen content following pulmonary oxygenation, rather than mixed venous oxygen content before gas exchange.

questions.stem: The central venous pressure, measured at the entrance to the right atrium, is normally about:
questions.why: Peripheral venous pressure is ~12-18 mmHg, falling to about 4-6 mmHg (CVP) at the right atrium.

questions.stem: Which mechanism helps return venous blood to the heart?
questions.why: Contracting skeletal muscles compress deep veins and displace blood towards the heart. Competent venous valves prevent backward flow during muscle relaxation, allowing repeated contractions to assist venous return against gravity.

notes.B: Standing upright increases hydrostatic pressure in dependent veins and promotes pooling, so gravity opposes return from the lower limbs.
notes.C: Arterial elastic recoil sustains arterial pressure and flow during diastole, but does not by itself provide the principal peripheral venous pumping mechanism.
notes.D: Venous valves open for forward flow and close against reverse flow; permanent closure would obstruct rather than facilitate venous return.
notes.E: Increased viscosity raises resistance to blood flow and can impede venous return for a given pressure gradient.

questions.stem: Veins are described as capacitance vessels because they:

options.label: B
options.text: hold a large reserve volume at low pressure

options.label: C
options.text: provide the main resistance to flow

questions.why: Veins are highly compliant vessels that accommodate a large proportion of circulating blood with relatively small changes in pressure. Venoconstriction can mobilise this reserve towards the heart when circulatory demand increases.

notes.A: High wall tension is not the defining feature of venous capacitance; veins normally store substantial blood volumes at relatively low pressure.
notes.C: Arterioles are the major adjustable resistance vessels because their small radii and smooth muscle tone strongly influence vascular resistance.
notes.D: Veins generally have thinner muscular walls than corresponding arteries, allowing greater distension and volume storage at low pressure.
notes.E: The arterial pulse originates from ventricular ejection and arterial wall distension, whereas venous capacitance refers to the storage of blood.

questions.stem: Heart failure is best defined as a state in which the heart cannot meet the metabolic needs of the tissues despite:

options.label: C
options.text: a normal or increased venous return

questions.why: The classical pump-failure concept distinguishes impaired cardiac performance from inadequate filling due solely to blood loss. Heart failure may involve inadequate output for tissue needs or adequate output maintained only at abnormally elevated filling pressures.

notes.A: Absent venous return prevents sustained cardiac output even in a structurally normal heart, rather than specifically establishing intrinsic cardiac pump failure.
notes.B: Severe anaemia reduces arterial oxygen content and may cause high-output heart failure, but anaemia is not a necessary feature of heart failure.
notes.D: Reduced venous return can lower output through inadequate preload even when the heart itself is functioning normally.
notes.E: Low circulating volume commonly causes hypovolaemic circulatory failure by reducing preload, rather than defining the classical condition of cardiac pump failure.

questions.stem: Backward failure of the LEFT heart characteristically produces:
questions.why: Impaired left ventricular emptying raises left ventricular filling pressure, left atrial pressure and pulmonary venous pressure. Increased pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure promotes fluid movement into lung interstitium and alveoli, producing dyspnoea and pulmonary oedema.

notes.A: Hepatomegaly from venous congestion is a characteristic consequence of raised systemic venous pressure in right-sided backward failure.
notes.B: Raised jugular venous pressure reflects elevated right atrial pressure and systemic venous congestion rather than isolated left-sided backward failure.
notes.C: Nocturnal diuresis may occur in heart failure as recumbency mobilises peripheral fluid, but it is not the characteristic direct pulmonary consequence.
notes.E: Peripheral oedema and ascites principally reflect systemic venous congestion, which characterises right-sided rather than isolated left-sided backward failure.

questions.stem: Backward failure of the RIGHT heart characteristically produces:
questions.why: Impaired right ventricular emptying raises right atrial and systemic venous pressures. Increased systemic capillary hydrostatic pressure produces dependent oedema, while hepatic venous congestion causes hepatomegaly and may contribute to ascites.

notes.A: Pulmonary oedema primarily results from raised pulmonary venous pressure in left-sided backward failure, rather than systemic venous congestion.
notes.B: Cardiac asthma describes wheezing associated with pulmonary congestion, typically caused by elevated left-sided filling pressures.
notes.C: Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea is classically associated with pulmonary congestion in left-sided heart failure, particularly after fluid redistribution during recumbency.
notes.D: Arterial hypoxaemia may accompany cardiopulmonary disease but does not specifically identify backward right-sided failure and systemic venous congestion.

questions.stem: Forward failure of the left heart mainly causes symptoms of:
questions.why: Forward left ventricular failure reduces effective systemic cardiac output and therefore tissue perfusion. Reduced oxygen delivery can cause fatigue and weakness, while diminished renal perfusion may produce oliguria and activate fluid-retaining mechanisms.

notes.B: Pulmonary congestion reflects elevated left atrial and pulmonary venous pressures, a backward rather than forward manifestation of left ventricular failure.
notes.C: Systemic venous congestion reflects elevated right-sided filling pressures rather than the direct reduction in systemic arterial output.
notes.D: Hepatic congestion develops when systemic venous pressure is transmitted into hepatic veins, principally reflecting right-sided backward failure.
notes.E: Peripheral oedema results partly from raised systemic venous and capillary pressures and is not the defining manifestation of forward left ventricular failure.

questions.stem: According to the Poiseuille-Hagen relationship, the resistance to blood flow is inversely proportional to the:
questions.why: For steady laminar flow through an ideal cylindrical tube, resistance equals eight times viscosity times length divided by pi times the fourth power of radius. Consequently, small changes in radius markedly alter resistance.

notes.A: Increasing blood viscosity increases frictional resistance to laminar flow, so resistance is directly rather than inversely proportional to viscosity.
notes.C: Resistance decreases as radius increases, but the ideal Poiseuille relationship involves the fourth power rather than a simple inverse relationship.
notes.D: The square of radius determines cross-sectional area, but the Poiseuille resistance relationship depends on the fourth power of radius.
notes.E: Increasing vessel length increases resistance by increasing the distance over which viscous friction acts; the relationship is directly proportional.

questions.stem: Halving the radius of a vessel, with all else constant, changes its resistance by a factor of:
questions.why: Poiseuille's relationship gives resistance proportional to one divided by radius to the fourth power. Replacing the original radius with half its value therefore multiplies resistance by two to the fourth power, or sixteen.

notes.A: An eightfold increase would follow an inverse cubic radius relationship, rather than the fourth-power dependence of Poiseuille resistance.
notes.B: A thirty-twofold increase corresponds to two raised to the fifth power, which is not the exponent in the resistance relationship.
notes.D: A twofold increase would occur if resistance were inversely proportional to radius alone, rather than its fourth power.
notes.E: A fourfold change describes the inverse cross-sectional area relationship when radius halves, not the sixteenfold change in Poiseuille resistance.

questions.stem: Blood flow through a vessel is directly proportional to the:
questions.why: The haemodynamic analogue of Ohm's law expresses flow as the pressure difference between the two ends of a vessel divided by resistance. At unchanged resistance, increasing the pressure gradient proportionally increases flow.

notes.A: Increasing vessel length raises resistance under Poiseuille conditions and therefore reduces flow when the driving pressure remains unchanged.
notes.B: Increasing viscosity increases viscous resistance and reduces flow for a fixed pressure difference, rather than increasing flow directly.
notes.C: Wall thickness can influence vessel mechanics and lumen size but does not directly determine flow in the basic pressure-gradient relationship.
notes.E: Increasing vascular resistance decreases flow at a fixed pressure gradient, so the relationship between flow and resistance is inverse.

questions.stem: The chief determinant of resistance to blood flow in the circulation is the:
questions.why: Vascular radius is the major adjustable determinant of resistance because Poiseuille resistance varies inversely with its fourth power. Arteriolar smooth muscle can therefore produce substantial changes in flow by modest changes in lumen radius.

notes.A: Blood viscosity influences resistance directly and varies with haematocrit, but radius has a much stronger fourth-power influence in the ideal relationship.
notes.B: Vessel length contributes directly to resistance but generally changes less rapidly than arteriolar radius during normal physiological regulation.
notes.C: Blood density influences inertial effects and Reynolds number, but is not the principal adjustable determinant of laminar vascular resistance.
notes.D: Flow velocity is an outcome of flow and cross-sectional area, although high velocity may promote turbulence and additional energy loss.

questions.stem: Turbulent blood flow, unlike laminar flow, is characterised by:
questions.why: Turbulent flow contains irregular velocity fluctuations and eddies that dissipate mechanical energy and may generate audible vibrations, such as vascular bruits or cardiac murmurs. Laminar flow is orderly and generally silent.

notes.B: A smooth, orderly and usually silent stream characterises laminar flow rather than the fluctuating motion of turbulent blood.
notes.C: Blood velocity approaches zero at a stationary vessel wall under the no-slip condition, rather than reaching its greatest value there.
notes.D: A parabolic velocity profile is characteristic of fully developed laminar flow of a Newtonian fluid through a cylindrical tube.
notes.E: Turbulence can occur wherever local velocity, geometry and fluid properties favour it, including narrow stenotic regions rather than exclusively large arteries.

questions.stem: A high Reynolds number, favouring turbulent flow, is promoted by:
questions.why: Reynolds number is proportional to fluid density, mean velocity and vessel diameter, and inversely proportional to dynamic viscosity. Increasing velocity therefore increases the tendency towards flow instability and turbulence, other factors being equal.

notes.A: Streamlined flow and smooth transitions reduce disturbances that can trigger turbulence, rather than directly increasing the Reynolds number.
notes.C: Increasing viscosity increases damping of velocity disturbances and lowers Reynolds number when other variables remain fixed.
notes.D: At fixed mean velocity, reducing vessel diameter lowers Reynolds number; a stenosis may nevertheless increase local velocity sufficiently to promote turbulence.
notes.E: Reducing blood density decreases Reynolds number at fixed velocity, diameter and viscosity, rather than promoting a higher value.

questions.stem: Blood velocity is highest in the aorta and lowest in the capillaries because the capillaries have the:
questions.why: Mean blood velocity equals volumetric flow divided by the combined cross-sectional area available to that flow. The enormous number of parallel capillaries produces a large total area, slowing blood movement and allowing time for exchange.

notes.A: Capillaries have very thin endothelial walls suited to exchange, and wall thickness does not explain their low mean blood velocity.
notes.B: Arterioles provide the major adjustable resistance; low capillary velocity is explained by the large combined area of the parallel capillary network.
notes.D: A smaller total cross-sectional area would increase mean velocity for unchanged volumetric flow, rather than explaining slow capillary blood movement.
notes.E: Capillary hydrostatic pressure is lower than aortic pressure after upstream resistance losses, and pressure alone does not explain the velocity minimum.

questions.stem: Blood viscosity depends chiefly on the:
questions.why: Haematocrit is the fraction of blood volume occupied by red cells and strongly influences whole-blood viscosity. A greater red cell concentration generally increases internal friction and viscosity, as occurs in polycythaemia.

notes.A: Heart rate changes the frequency of pulsatile blood flow but does not principally determine the intrinsic viscosity of whole blood.
notes.B: Vessel length influences hydraulic resistance, not the viscosity of the blood flowing through the vessel.
notes.C: Arterial pressure helps drive flow, while blood viscosity is principally determined by cellular concentration, plasma properties and shear conditions.
notes.E: Plasma sodium affects osmolality and can influence cell volume, but haematocrit is the major conventional determinant of whole-blood viscosity.

questions.stem: Autoregulation of blood flow is the capacity of a tissue to:

options.label: E
options.text: keep its own blood flow nearly constant

questions.why: Autoregulation allows a tissue to maintain relatively stable blood flow over a range of perfusion pressures by adjusting local arteriolar resistance. Myogenic and metabolic mechanisms help match perfusion to tissue requirements.

notes.A: Systemic blood pressure is regulated through integrated cardiovascular mechanisms, whereas autoregulation specifically adjusts local resistance to stabilise tissue blood flow.
notes.B: Heart rate is regulated primarily through cardiac pacemaker and autonomic mechanisms rather than local tissue autoregulation.
notes.C: Blood viscosity is a property of circulating blood; local autoregulation chiefly changes vascular smooth muscle tone rather than blood composition.
notes.D: Cardiac output is total ventricular flow per minute, whereas autoregulation concerns the distribution and stability of flow within an individual tissue.

questions.stem: By the metabolic theory of autoregulation, a fall in local blood flow leads to:
questions.why: Reduced local perfusion decreases the removal of vasodilator metabolites and may reduce oxygen delivery. The resulting arteriolar relaxation lowers resistance and helps restore tissue blood flow through metabolic autoregulation.

notes.B: Metabolite washout increases when perfusion rises, reducing local vasodilator concentrations and favouring restoration of vascular resistance.
notes.C: Myogenic contraction is a response to increased vascular wall stretch, whereas metabolic autoregulation responds to changes in local tissue chemistry.
notes.D: Serotonin can influence vascular tone through receptor-dependent effects, but its release is not the principal metabolic response to reduced tissue perfusion.
notes.E: Reflex bradycardia changes systemic cardiac output and is not the local mechanism through which an underperfused tissue dilates its arterioles.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a local metabolic VASODILATOR?
questions.why: Adenosine accumulates during ATP breakdown when metabolic activity increases or oxygen supply becomes inadequate. It relaxes vascular smooth muscle in several systemic vascular beds, particularly the coronary circulation, helping match perfusion to demand.

notes.A: Vasopressin acts on vascular V1 receptors to promote vasoconstriction rather than serving as a typical local vasodilator metabolite.
notes.C: Serotonin has receptor-dependent vascular effects, including constriction in several vascular beds, rather than being the classic metabolic dilator associated with ATP breakdown.
notes.D: Angiotensin II activates vascular AT1 receptors and generally increases vascular resistance through smooth muscle contraction.
notes.E: Cold commonly promotes cutaneous vasoconstriction to conserve body heat; it is a thermal stimulus rather than a locally generated metabolic vasodilator.

questions.stem: Endothelium-derived relaxing factor, which mediates vasodilatation by substances such as bradykinin, is:
questions.why: Nitric oxide is synthesised by endothelial nitric oxide synthase in response to stimuli including bradykinin and shear stress. It diffuses into vascular smooth muscle, activates soluble guanylyl cyclase and increases cGMP-dependent relaxation.

notes.A: Endothelin is an endothelial peptide that usually causes powerful vasoconstriction through smooth muscle endothelin A receptors, unlike the classic relaxing factor.
notes.B: Serotonin is a vasoactive monoamine with receptor-dependent effects; it is not the molecule originally identified as endothelium-derived relaxing factor.
notes.D: Histamine can stimulate endothelial nitric oxide production and promote vasodilatation, but it is not itself the classic endothelium-derived relaxing factor.
notes.E: Angiotensin II is a major renin–angiotensin system effector that usually causes vasoconstriction rather than mediating nitric oxide-dependent smooth muscle relaxation.

questions.stem: The myogenic theory of autoregulation holds that vascular smooth muscle contracts in response to:

options.label: A
options.text: a fall in the oxygen tension

questions.why: An increase in transmural pressure stretches vascular smooth muscle and activates intrinsic mechanosensitive signalling, including membrane depolarisation and calcium entry. The resulting contraction increases resistance and limits excessive blood flow.

notes.A: Reduced oxygen tension usually promotes metabolic vasodilatation in systemic tissues, rather than triggering the stretch-dependent myogenic response.
notes.B: Increased local temperature can influence vascular tone through thermal and metabolic mechanisms, but it is not the defining myogenic stimulus.
notes.C: Parasympathetic discharge can influence selected vascular beds through neural mechanisms; myogenic autoregulation is intrinsic to vascular smooth muscle.
notes.E: Accumulating vasodilator metabolites favour relaxation through metabolic autoregulation, rather than defining the contraction induced by increased wall stretch.

questions.stem: By the law of Laplace, for a given wall tension the distending pressure a vessel can withstand is greater when its radius is:
questions.why: For an ideal thin-walled cylindrical vessel, circumferential wall tension equals transmural pressure multiplied by radius. Rearranging gives pressure as tension divided by radius, so a smaller radius permits a higher pressure at the same tension.

notes.A: A larger radius requires greater circumferential tension to balance the same transmural pressure, rather than permitting higher pressure at fixed tension.
notes.B: An unchanged radius leaves the pressure–tension relationship unchanged when wall tension is fixed, so it does not increase the supported pressure.
notes.C: Wall thickness matters when converting wall tension into wall stress, but equality of radius and thickness is not required for the Laplace relationship.
notes.D: Maximum stretch generally increases vessel radius, which would reduce the pressure supported at a specified fixed circumferential wall tension.

questions.stem: Pulse pressure is defined as the:

options.label: A
options.text: difference between systolic and diastolic pressure

options.label: C
options.text: diastolic pressure plus one-third of systolic

options.label: E
options.text: sum of systolic and diastolic pressure

questions.why: Pulse pressure is systolic arterial pressure minus diastolic arterial pressure. It represents the amplitude of the arterial pressure oscillation and is influenced particularly by stroke volume and arterial compliance.

notes.B: The time-averaged arterial pressure over a cardiac cycle is mean arterial pressure, not the difference between its peak and trough.
notes.C: Adding a fraction of systolic pressure to diastolic pressure does not define pulse pressure; pulse pressure requires subtracting diastolic pressure from systolic pressure.
notes.D: Systolic pressure minus mean pressure measures only the pressure excursion above the mean, rather than the complete peak-to-trough difference.
notes.E: Adding systolic and diastolic pressures produces a sum, not the amplitude of the arterial pressure change during a heartbeat.

questions.stem: Mean arterial pressure is estimated as:

options.label: B
options.text: diastolic pressure plus one-third of the pulse pressure

options.label: C
options.text: the average of systolic and diastolic pressure

options.label: E
options.text: diastolic pressure plus the pulse pressure

questions.why: At a normal resting heart rate, mean arterial pressure is approximated by diastolic pressure plus one-third of pulse pressure. The weighting reflects the longer time spent in diastole than systole; it changes at higher heart rates.

notes.A: Subtracting systolic pressure from twice diastolic pressure incorrectly reduces the estimate as systolic pressure rises at constant diastolic pressure.
notes.C: The simple arithmetic average gives equal weighting to systolic and diastolic pressures, overlooking the longer duration of diastole at rest.
notes.D: Systolic minus diastolic pressure defines pulse pressure, which measures pressure amplitude rather than the time-averaged arterial pressure.
notes.E: Adding the entire pulse pressure to diastolic pressure simply recovers systolic pressure, rather than estimating the mean over the cardiac cycle.

questions.stem: Maintenance of arterial pressure during diastole, by elastic recoil of the large arteries, is known as the:
questions.why: The Windkessel effect reflects the ability of elastic arteries to store part of ventricular stroke volume and elastic energy during systole. Their recoil during diastole maintains arterial pressure and forward flow despite intermittent ventricular ejection.

notes.A: The Valsalva manoeuvre alters intrathoracic pressure, venous return and reflex cardiovascular responses, rather than describing arterial elastic energy storage.
notes.B: The Anrep effect describes a delayed increase in myocardial contractile force after increased loading, not elastic recoil of the arterial tree.
notes.D: The Bernoulli principle relates pressure, velocity and elevation in fluid flow; it does not describe the arterial reservoir function during diastole.
notes.E: The Bainbridge reflex describes a heart-rate response to increased atrial stretch and venous return, not the maintenance of diastolic arterial pressure.

questions.stem: The first Korotkoff sound heard while deflating a blood-pressure cuff corresponds to the:
questions.why: As cuff pressure falls just below peak arterial pressure, blood begins passing intermittently through the compressed artery during systole. The first audible Korotkoff sounds therefore estimate systolic pressure during auscultatory measurement.

notes.A: Mean arterial pressure is the time-averaged arterial pressure; oscillometric devices estimate it from cuff oscillations rather than the first Korotkoff sound.
notes.B: Pulse pressure requires the difference between separately measured systolic and diastolic pressures, not the pressure at the first audible sound alone.
notes.C: Venous pressure is considerably lower than arterial systolic pressure and is not the quantity measured at the onset of Korotkoff sounds.
notes.E: Diastolic pressure is generally estimated at disappearance of Korotkoff sounds in adults, rather than at their first appearance.

questions.stem: Using a cuff that is too SMALL for the arm gives a reading that is falsely:
questions.why: An undersized blood pressure cuff requires excessive cuff pressure to compress the underlying brachial artery adequately. This commonly overestimates systolic and diastolic pressures, making correct cuff sizing important for accurate measurement.

notes.A: An excessively large cuff tends to underestimate blood pressure, whereas an undersized cuff generally produces the opposite error.
notes.B: Incorrect cuff size changes the relationship between applied cuff pressure and arterial compression, so the reading is not reliably unaffected.
notes.C: An undersized cuff commonly still produces measurable sounds or oscillations, but the recorded pressure is biased rather than necessarily absent.
notes.D: Although the size of the error varies among individuals, the characteristic direction of bias from an undersized cuff is upward.

questions.stem: When measuring blood pressure, the cuff must be positioned at the level of the:
questions.why: The upper-arm cuff should be supported at approximately right atrial level to minimise hydrostatic pressure error. A cuff below heart level tends to read too high, whereas one above heart level tends to read too low.

notes.B: Shoulder height is not the standard reference and may position the cuff above right atrial level, introducing a hydrostatic underestimate.
notes.C: Wrist height varies with limb position; even wrist-based measurements require the device to be held at heart level.
notes.D: Neck level is generally above the right atrium in an upright individual, so it is not the appropriate hydrostatic reference.
notes.E: Mid-thigh level is generally below the right atrium when seated or standing and would introduce a hydrostatic pressure difference.

questions.stem: The main integrating centre controlling arteriolar tone and blood pressure is located in the:
questions.why: Medullary cardiovascular networks integrate baroreceptor and other afferent signals and regulate sympathetic vasomotor activity. In particular, the nucleus tractus solitarius and ventrolateral medullary regions participate in controlling arteriolar resistance and arterial pressure.

notes.A: The cerebellum primarily coordinates movement and balance, although it can influence autonomic functions indirectly rather than serving as the main vasomotor centre.
notes.C: The cerebral cortex can modify cardiovascular responses during emotion and voluntary activity, but basic reflex integration occurs chiefly within the brainstem.
notes.D: The hypothalamus coordinates autonomic responses to temperature, stress and homeostatic demands, while the medulla provides major cardiovascular reflex integration.
notes.E: The spinal cord contains sympathetic preganglionic neurons that transmit vasomotor commands, but major baroreflex integration occurs in medullary circuits.

questions.stem: Blood vessels receive a continuous (tonic) discharge from which fibres?
questions.why: Most systemic resistance vessels receive tonic sympathetic vasoconstrictor activity. Noradrenaline released from postganglionic fibres activates vascular alpha-adrenergic receptors, allowing changes in sympathetic discharge to increase or decrease basal vascular tone.

notes.A: Somatic motor fibres activate skeletal muscle at neuromuscular junctions rather than supplying the usual tonic constrictor input to vascular smooth muscle.
notes.B: Sensory afferents carry information towards the central nervous system and are not the principal efferent fibres maintaining systemic vascular tone.
notes.D: Parasympathetic vasodilator innervation is limited to selected tissues and does not supply the widespread tonic constrictor activity of systemic resistance vessels.
notes.E: Sympathetic vasodilator mechanisms exist in selected contexts, but widespread basal neurogenic vascular tone is predominantly maintained by sympathetic vasoconstrictor fibres.

questions.stem: Sympathetic vasodilator fibres to vessels in skeletal muscle are unusual in that they are:
questions.why: Sympathetic vasodilator fibres (to muscle and liver) release acetylcholine - they are cholinergic.

questions.stem: Sympathetic stimulation of the heart produces a:

options.label: B
options.text: rise in rate but fall in force

options.label: C
options.text: fall in rate but rise in force

options.label: D
options.text: no change in rate or force

options.label: E
options.text: rise in both rate and force

questions.why: Sympathetic noradrenaline stimulates cardiac beta-1 receptors, increasing cAMP-dependent pacemaker activity and calcium handling. This increases both heart rate through positive chronotropy and myocardial contractility through positive inotropy.

notes.A: A reduction in rate is characteristic of vagal stimulation, whereas cardiac sympathetic activation normally accelerates sinoatrial firing and increases contraction strength.
notes.B: Sympathetic stimulation increases calcium-dependent myocardial force alongside heart rate, rather than producing the combination of tachycardia and reduced contractility.
notes.C: Increased contractile force is consistent with sympathetic stimulation, but sinoatrial firing normally accelerates rather than slowing during direct beta-1 activation.
notes.D: Cardiac sympathetic input modifies both pacemaker activity and contractile performance, so it does not normally leave both variables unchanged.

questions.stem: Resting heart rate is held down mainly by:

options.label: D
options.text: the intrinsic SA node rate alone

questions.why: At rest, tonic parasympathetic activity releases acetylcholine onto sinoatrial M2 receptors and slows spontaneous pacemaker depolarisation. This keeps resting heart rate below the intrinsic sinoatrial rate, which becomes more apparent after autonomic blockade.

notes.B: Tonic sympathetic discharge accelerates sinoatrial firing through beta-1 receptors and therefore opposes, rather than explains, the resting vagal slowing.
notes.C: Circulating adrenaline generally stimulates cardiac beta-adrenergic receptors and increases heart rate, rather than maintaining the resting rate below intrinsic pacemaker frequency.
notes.D: The intrinsic sinoatrial rate is generally higher than the usual resting heart rate because autonomic activity, especially vagal tone, modifies it.
notes.E: Atrial stretch can increase heart rate through the Bainbridge reflex, but it is not the predominant mechanism restraining resting sinoatrial firing.

questions.stem: Atrial natriuretic peptide acts on the vasculature to cause:
questions.why: Atrial natriuretic peptide is released in response to atrial stretch and activates natriuretic peptide receptor A, increasing intracellular cGMP. It promotes vascular relaxation and renal sodium excretion, helping reduce circulatory volume and pressure.

notes.A: Venoconstriction mobilises stored venous blood towards the heart, whereas atrial natriuretic peptide generally favours reduced vascular tone and volume.
notes.C: Vasoconstriction increases vascular resistance, while atrial natriuretic peptide typically activates cGMP-mediated smooth muscle relaxation and opposes pressor systems.
notes.D: Increased myocardial contractility is chiefly associated with positive inotropic signalling, not the primary vascular action of atrial natriuretic peptide.
notes.E: Tachycardia may result from autonomic reflexes, but atrial natriuretic peptide primarily promotes vasodilatation and natriuresis rather than directly accelerating pacemaker firing.

questions.stem: The arterial baroreceptors are located in the carotid sinus and the:
questions.why: High-pressure arterial baroreceptors are stretch-sensitive endings located principally in the carotid sinuses and aortic arch. They detect changes in arterial wall distension and send afferent signals to medullary cardiovascular centres.

notes.A: The right atrium contains cardiopulmonary receptors responsive to filling and stretch, rather than the principal high-pressure systemic arterial baroreceptors.
notes.B: Receptors near the caval–atrial junction can monitor venous filling, but the superior vena cava is not a principal high-pressure arterial baroreceptor site.
notes.D: The pulmonary circulation contains cardiopulmonary sensory receptors, but the classic systemic arterial baroreflex arises chiefly from carotid sinus and aortic arch receptors.
notes.E: The coronary sinus drains myocardial venous blood into the right atrium and is not a principal high-pressure arterial baroreceptor location.

questions.stem: Afferent impulses from the carotid sinus baroreceptors travel to the medulla in the:
questions.why: Carotid sinus stretch signals travel through the carotid sinus nerve, also called Hering's nerve, which joins the glossopharyngeal nerve. These afferents terminate in the medullary nucleus tractus solitarius.

notes.A: The phrenic nerve supplies the diaphragm and carries associated sensory signals; it does not transmit carotid sinus baroreceptor afferents.
notes.B: The trigeminal nerve carries facial sensation and supplies muscles of mastication, rather than providing the principal carotid sinus afferent pathway.
notes.C: The hypoglossal nerve supplies tongue musculature and is not the sensory pathway from carotid sinus baroreceptors.
notes.E: The vagus nerve carries aortic arch baroreceptor afferents and other visceral sensory signals, whereas carotid sinus afferents primarily travel through the glossopharyngeal nerve.

questions.stem: A sudden RISE in arterial pressure triggers a baroreceptor reflex that causes:

options.label: A
options.text: speeding of the heart and vasoconstriction

options.label: E
options.text: slowing of the heart and vasodilatation

questions.why: Increased arterial pressure stretches baroreceptors and increases their afferent firing. Medullary integration enhances cardiac vagal activity and reduces sympathetic activity, slowing the heart and dilating resistance vessels to oppose the pressure rise.

notes.A: Tachycardia and vasoconstriction are compensatory responses to reduced arterial pressure, rather than the normal baroreflex response to a pressure rise.
notes.B: Increased arterial baroreceptor firing inhibits sympathetic vasomotor output, rather than increasing the sympathetic activity that would support a further pressure rise.
notes.C: Reduced heart rate and sympathetic cardiac stimulation tend to decrease cardiac output during this reflex, rather than actively increase it.
notes.D: Reduced sympathetic activity generally relaxes capacitance veins, whereas venoconstriction is more characteristic of compensation for falling arterial pressure.

questions.stem: A FALL in arterial pressure produces a reflex that leads to:
questions.why: A fall in arterial pressure reduces carotid sinus and aortic arch stretch, decreasing baroreceptor firing. The resulting increase in sympathetic activity and withdrawal of vagal activity accelerate the heart and constrict vessels to support pressure.

notes.B: Bradycardia and vasodilatation are typical compensatory responses to raised arterial pressure and would worsen an existing pressure fall.
notes.C: Reduced baroreceptor firing disinhibits sympathetic vasomotor pathways, increasing rather than reducing sympathetic output during an acute pressure fall.
notes.D: Slowing the heart would tend to reduce cardiac output; vagal withdrawal normally accelerates sinoatrial firing during baroreflex compensation for hypotension.
