notes.E: Sympathetic arteriolar constriction raises peripheral resistance during compensation, rather than producing a further fall in vascular resistance.

questions.stem: The Cushing reflex, triggered by raised intracranial pressure, classically produces:

options.label: A
options.text: no change in pressure or rate

questions.why: Markedly raised intracranial pressure can compromise cerebral perfusion, triggering a sympathetic pressor response that increases systemic arterial pressure. The arterial baroreflex then produces bradycardia; irregular respiration completes the classical Cushing triad.

notes.A: A significant Cushing response changes systemic arterial pressure and heart rate as the body attempts to maintain cerebral perfusion.
notes.C: Hypotension with tachycardia is more typical of compensation for reduced systemic circulating volume than the classical Cushing response to raised intracranial pressure.
notes.D: The sympathetic pressor response raises arterial pressure, but subsequent baroreceptor activation characteristically slows rather than accelerates the heart.
notes.E: Hypotension would further compromise cerebral perfusion, whereas the classic Cushing response includes a compensatory rise in systemic arterial pressure.

questions.stem: The vasomotor centre is directly stimulated by:
questions.why: Hypoxia and hypercapnia directly excite the vasomotor centre, raising sympathetic output.

questions.stem: On standing, blood tends to pool in the dependent veins; the resulting fall in arterial pressure is sensed by the:

options.label: D
options.text: aortic arch and carotid sinus receptors

questions.why: Standing promotes dependent venous pooling and transiently reduces ventricular filling, stroke volume and arterial pressure. Carotid sinus and aortic arch baroreceptors detect the reduction in arterial stretch and initiate rapid compensatory cardiovascular responses.

notes.A: Pulmonary stretch receptors chiefly monitor lung inflation and participate in respiratory reflexes, rather than directly sensing systemic arterial pressure.
notes.B: Peripheral chemoreceptors respond primarily to arterial oxygen, carbon dioxide and hydrogen ion changes, whereas baroreceptors detect arterial wall stretch.
notes.C: Joint proprioceptors provide information about limb position and movement, rather than directly monitoring the acute reduction in systemic arterial pressure.
notes.E: Atrial low-pressure receptors detect changes in central blood volume and contribute to cardiovascular regulation, but arterial pressure is directly sensed by arterial baroreceptors.

questions.stem: Orthostatic (postural) hypotension is characteristically due to failure of:
questions.why: Normal standing evokes sympathetic arteriolar and venous constriction that limits pooling and supports arterial pressure. Impaired autonomic vasoconstriction can produce neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, although volume depletion and other non-neurogenic causes are also common.

notes.A: Parasympathetic withdrawal contributes to compensatory tachycardia, but the major vascular defect in neurogenic orthostatic hypotension involves inadequate sympathetic vasoconstriction.
notes.B: The respiratory pump assists venous return, but failure of this mechanism is not the characteristic autonomic abnormality in neurogenic orthostatic hypotension.
notes.C: Abnormal pacemaker activity can reduce cardiac output, but impaired sympathetic vascular compensation is the characteristic mechanism of neurogenic postural hypotension.
notes.D: Renal sodium handling influences circulating volume over longer periods, whereas rapid postural compensation relies strongly on sympathetic vascular responses.

questions.stem: During exposure to high positive (+Gz) acceleration, loss of vision ('black-out') occurs because of:
questions.why: Positive g drives blood footward, reducing cerebral perfusion so that vision fails and consciousness is lost.

questions.stem: A pressure ('g') suit improves tolerance to acceleration by:

options.label: B
options.text: compressing the legs to limit pooling

questions.why: A positive-acceleration pressure suit compresses the lower limbs and often the abdomen, limiting dependent venous pooling and helping maintain central blood volume. This supports arterial pressure and perfusion of the brain and eyes.

notes.A: Reducing intracranial pressure is not the primary action of a pressure suit, which chiefly limits acceleration-induced blood redistribution towards the lower body.
notes.C: Heart rate may change through compensatory reflexes, but the suit primarily acts mechanically on lower-body circulation rather than directly stimulating the sinoatrial node.
notes.D: Cerebral vasodilatation may assist local autoregulation, but the suit preserves perfusion mainly by limiting lower-body pooling and maintaining central arterial pressure.
notes.E: Increasing viscosity would raise resistance to blood flow, whereas a pressure suit works by mechanically compressing dependent vascular compartments.

questions.stem: Circulatory shock is best defined as:

options.label: B
options.text: loss of consciousness from any cause

options.label: D
options.text: a sustained rise in arterial pressure

questions.why: Circulatory shock is acute circulatory failure in which tissue perfusion and oxygen delivery or utilisation become inadequate for metabolic requirements. It can result from volume loss, pump failure, obstruction or abnormal distribution of blood flow.

notes.A: Respiratory failure impairs gas exchange and may worsen tissue oxygen delivery, but does not by itself define acute circulatory failure.
notes.B: Loss of consciousness can arise from neurological, metabolic or circulatory causes and is neither necessary nor sufficient to diagnose shock.
notes.D: A sustained rise in arterial pressure defines hypertension, whereas shock concerns inadequate tissue perfusion and may occur even before hypotension develops.
notes.E: Bradycardia can contribute to reduced cardiac output, but shock also occurs with normal or elevated heart rates and has multiple circulatory mechanisms.

questions.stem: Shock due to haemorrhage, burns or severe vomiting is classified as:
questions.why: Haemorrhage reduces circulating blood volume, while burns and severe vomiting can cause substantial intravascular fluid depletion. Reduced venous return and preload lower stroke volume and cardiac output, producing hypovolaemic shock when compensation becomes inadequate.

notes.A: Distributive shock primarily involves abnormal vascular tone and blood-flow distribution, rather than the primary loss of circulating volume described here.
notes.B: Obstructive shock results from mechanical impairment of cardiac filling or blood flow, such as tamponade or massive pulmonary embolism.
notes.C: Neurogenic shock results from loss of sympathetic vascular tone, typically after significant spinal cord injury, rather than primary blood or fluid loss.
notes.E: Cardiogenic shock primarily results from inadequate myocardial pumping, whereas the listed conditions predominantly reduce the volume available to fill the heart.

questions.stem: Shock caused by cardiac tamponade or massive pulmonary embolism is classified as:
questions.why: Cardiac tamponade restricts diastolic filling through elevated pericardial pressure, whereas massive pulmonary embolism obstructs pulmonary blood flow and increases right ventricular load. Both mechanically impair effective cardiac output and can produce obstructive shock.

notes.A: Hypovolaemic shock results primarily from reduced circulating volume rather than a mechanical impediment to cardiac filling or pulmonary blood flow.
notes.B: Distributive shock principally involves abnormal vascular tone and maldistribution of perfusion, rather than the mechanical obstruction described by these conditions.
notes.C: Cardiogenic shock is primarily due to intrinsic cardiac pump dysfunction; tamponade and pulmonary embolism are conventionally classified as mechanical obstructive causes.
notes.D: Anaphylactic shock involves mediator-induced vasodilatation and vascular permeability, rather than direct compression of the heart or obstruction of pulmonary arterial flow.

questions.stem: In early hypovolaemic shock the skin is typically pale and cool because of:

options.label: C
options.text: a rise in the cardiac output

questions.why: Acute volume loss decreases arterial baroreceptor firing and increases sympathetic vasoconstrictor activity. Constriction of cutaneous resistance vessels reduces skin perfusion, producing pallor and coolness while helping preserve arterial pressure and vital-organ perfusion.

notes.B: Cutaneous vasodilatation increases skin blood flow and may produce warm skin, rather than explaining the cool pallor typical of compensated hypovolaemia.
notes.C: Cardiac output generally falls as volume loss reduces preload; compensatory mechanisms may partially maintain output but do not directly explain cutaneous pallor.
notes.D: Loss of vasomotor tone would favour vasodilatation, whereas the characteristic early compensatory response to hypovolaemia is increased sympathetic vascular tone.
notes.E: Histamine promotes local vasodilatation and increased permeability, rather than mediating the baroreceptor-driven cutaneous vasoconstriction of early hypovolaemic shock.

questions.stem: During shock, blood flow is preferentially preserved to the:
questions.why: During compensated shock, sympathetic vasoconstriction redistributes blood away from several peripheral and splanchnic beds. Strong local metabolic and autoregulatory mechanisms help preserve myocardial and cerebral perfusion, although severe or prolonged shock eventually compromises these organs.

notes.A: Skeletal muscle flow may decrease through sympathetic vasoconstriction during resting compensated shock, allowing limited circulating flow to support more immediately vital organs.
notes.C: Cutaneous and renal perfusion commonly decrease during compensatory sympathetic activation; cool skin and reduced urine output may reflect this redistribution.
notes.D: Splanchnic and skeletal muscle vascular beds can undergo vasoconstriction during compensation, rather than receiving the principal preferential preservation of flow.
notes.E: Hepatic and splenic perfusion can decline during circulatory shock as sympathetic responses redistribute available blood towards critical cardiac and cerebral requirements.

questions.stem: Distributive (low-resistance) shock, such as septic or anaphylactic shock, is characterised by:
questions.why: Distributive shock involves abnormally low vascular tone and maldistributed tissue perfusion. Widespread vasodilatation increases vascular capacity and reduces effective filling, while capillary leakage may additionally cause actual intravascular volume depletion in sepsis or anaphylaxis.

notes.A: Primary myocardial pump failure characterises cardiogenic shock, although myocardial dysfunction may coexist with distributive shock in severe sepsis.
notes.B: Acute haemorrhage primarily reduces circulating volume and causes hypovolaemic shock, rather than the characteristic widespread loss of vascular tone.
notes.D: Reduced intravascular volume can accompany distributive shock through capillary leakage, but vasodilatation and maldistribution are its distinguishing primary mechanisms.
notes.E: Mechanical obstruction to cardiac filling or outflow characterises obstructive shock rather than the vascular tone abnormality defining distributive shock.

questions.stem: Vasovagal syncope (simple fainting) is caused by:
questions.why: Vasovagal syncope results from reflex-mediated hypotension, often involving vasodilatation and inappropriate slowing of the heart. The transient reduction in global cerebral perfusion produces brief loss of consciousness with spontaneous recovery when perfusion returns.

notes.A: Cerebral haemorrhage causes neurological injury through bleeding and is not the reflex mechanism responsible for uncomplicated vasovagal syncope.
notes.B: Airway obstruction impairs ventilation and oxygenation, whereas vasovagal syncope primarily results from transient inadequate cerebral blood flow.
notes.C: Hypoglycaemia deprives the brain of glucose and may impair consciousness, but does not define the reflex circulatory mechanism of vasovagal syncope.
notes.E: A primary cardiac arrhythmia can cause cardiac syncope by reducing output, whereas vasovagal syncope arises from an abnormal autonomic reflex.

questions.stem: The wall of a typical capillary consists of:

options.label: E
options.text: a single layer of endothelial cells

questions.why: A typical capillary wall consists of a single layer of endothelial cells supported by a basal lamina, with pericytes associated with some capillaries. The thin barrier facilitates exchange between blood and surrounding tissues.

notes.A: Smooth muscle surrounding endothelial cells characterises arterioles and some larger microvessels; typical capillaries do not possess a continuous smooth muscle coat.
notes.B: Three distinct tunicae characterise larger arteries and veins, whereas capillaries lack separate muscular and adventitial coats.
notes.C: Elastic laminae are structural features of larger arteries and are not present as distinct layers in a typical capillary wall.
notes.D: A thick collagenous coat would increase diffusion distance; typical capillaries instead possess a thin endothelial barrier with basal lamina support.

questions.stem: Blood flow into a capillary bed is controlled by:
questions.why: Precapillary sphincters (smooth muscle, responding to local substances rather than nerves) regulate capillary flow.

questions.stem: Fenestrations in capillary endothelium, allowing passage of larger molecules, are especially prominent in the:
questions.why: Fenestrated capillaries occur where exchange is high - kidney, intestinal villi and endocrine glands; brain capillaries are non-fenestrated.

questions.stem: According to Starling's forces, the main pressure driving fluid OUT of the capillary is the:
questions.why: Capillary hydrostatic pressure drives filtration out; plasma oncotic pressure draws fluid back in.

questions.stem: Of the fluid filtered out of the capillaries each day, the proportion returned to the circulation by the lymphatics is about:
questions.why: About 85% of filtered fluid is reabsorbed by capillaries and roughly 15% is returned via lymph.

questions.stem: Oedema is an abnormal accumulation of fluid in the:
questions.why: Oedema is excess fluid in the interstitium, from increased filtration or inadequate reabsorption/drainage.

questions.stem: A fall in plasma protein concentration (as in liver disease, nephrotic syndrome or malnutrition) causes oedema by:

options.label: A
options.text: lowering the plasma colloid osmotic pressure

questions.why: Low plasma proteins reduce the oncotic pull back into capillaries, so fluid stays in the interstitium.

questions.stem: Non-pitting oedema (lymphoedema), as in elephantiasis after filarial infection, is caused by:
questions.why: Lymphatic obstruction (e.g. filarial worms, radical mastectomy) causes protein-rich, non-pitting lymphoedema.

questions.stem: The lymphatic vessels ultimately return lymph to the bloodstream at the:

options.label: E
options.text: the right atrium of the heart

questions.why: Lymph drains into the venous system at the subclavian veins (right and left).

questions.stem: Lymph flow along the vessels is aided by all of the following EXCEPT:

options.label: B
options.text: rhythmic contractions of the vessel wall

options.label: D
options.text: direct pumping of lymph by the heart

questions.why: Lymph is moved by the muscle pump, thoracic pump, wall contractions and valves - not by direct cardiac pumping.

questions.stem: An important function of the lymphatic system is the:

options.label: C
options.text: production of the red blood cells

options.label: E
options.text: returning filtered protein to the blood

questions.why: Lymphatics return filtered interstitial protein (and absorbed fat) to the blood.

questions.stem: The coronary arteries arise from the:
questions.why: The right and left coronary arteries arise from the aortic sinuses behind the aortic valve cusps.

questions.stem: Coronary blood flow to the left ventricular myocardium occurs mainly during:
questions.why: During systole the intramural vessels are compressed, so left ventricular coronary flow occurs chiefly in diastole.

questions.stem: Angina pectoris on exertion typically occurs when a coronary artery is narrowed by about:
questions.why: Flow is adequate at rest but inadequate on exertion once a vessel is ~75% occluded, causing angina.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a potent metabolic coronary VASODILATOR?
questions.why: Adenosine (with O2 lack, K+, H+, CO2, lactate) dilates coronary vessels during increased cardiac work.

questions.stem: The arterial anastomosis at the base of the brain is the:
questions.why: The circle of Willis links the internal carotid and vertebrobasilar supplies at the brain's base.

questions.stem: Cerebrospinal fluid is produced mainly by the:
questions.why: CSF is secreted mainly by the choroid plexuses of the lateral, third and fourth ventricles.

questions.stem: Cerebrospinal fluid is absorbed back into the venous blood through the:
questions.why: CSF passes into the subarachnoid space and is absorbed through the arachnoid villi into the dural sinuses.

questions.stem: The Monro-Kellie doctrine states that the sum of the volumes of brain, CSF and which other component is constant within the rigid skull?
questions.why: The cranial contents - brain, CSF and blood - have a near-constant total volume (Monro-Kellie doctrine).

questions.stem: The blood-brain barrier allows easy passage of:
questions.why: Small, lipid-soluble, non-polar molecules cross easily; proteins and protein-bound substances do not.

questions.stem: An ischaemic stroke is most often caused by:

options.label: B
options.text: a fall in the CSF pressure

options.label: D
options.text: a rise in the venous pressure

options.label: E
options.text: a thrombus or embolus in an artery

questions.why: Ischaemic stroke results from arterial occlusion (atherosclerotic thrombus or embolus); haemorrhagic stroke from vessel rupture.

questions.stem: Compared with the systemic circulation, the pulmonary circulation is a:
questions.why: The pulmonary circulation operates at low pressure (~10 mmHg capillary) and low resistance.

questions.stem: In the lung, alveolar hypoxia causes the local pulmonary vessels to:
questions.why: Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction diverts blood from poorly ventilated areas to better-oxygenated ones.

questions.stem: The low hydrostatic pressure in pulmonary capillaries is important because it:

options.label: C
options.text: keeps fluid from accumulating in the alveoli

options.label: D
options.text: raises the work of the right heart

questions.why: Low pulmonary capillary pressure (below plasma oncotic pressure) keeps the alveoli dry.

questions.stem: On lying down, the volume of blood held in the lungs:
questions.why: The lungs act as a blood reservoir; lying down adds about 400 ml to the pulmonary circulation.

questions.stem: The three unpaired arteries supplying the splanchnic (gut) circulation are the celiac trunk, the superior mesenteric artery and the:
questions.why: The gut is supplied by the celiac trunk and the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries.

questions.stem: During shock or heavy sympathetic discharge, the splanchnic circulation characteristically:

options.label: A
options.text: constricts and releases its stored blood

options.label: B
options.text: dilates further to store more blood

questions.why: The splanchnic bed is a large venous reservoir; in shock it constricts and shifts blood to the vital circulations.

questions.stem: Within the liver lobule, blood flows from the portal triad towards the:
questions.why: Blood flows from the triad through the sinusoids to the central vein; the perivenous zone is least oxygenated.

questions.stem: In the formation of ascites, the protein-rich fluid leaking from the liver is explained by the fact that hepatic sinusoids:

options.label: C
options.text: have pores permeable to plasma protein

questions.why: Sinusoidal pores let protein into the space of Disse; raised hepatic venous pressure then drives protein-rich fluid out as ascites.

questions.stem: The main physiological role of the cutaneous circulation is:
questions.why: Skin blood flow, with its many anastomoses, is primarily for heat exchange and thermoregulation.

questions.stem: In the triple response of the skin, the spreading redness ('flare') around an injury is due to:

options.label: E
options.text: arteriolar dilatation via an axon reflex

questions.why: The flare is arteriolar dilatation spreading by an antidromic axon reflex; the wheal is local oedema from increased permeability.

questions.stem: The initial 'white reaction' after lightly stroking the skin is caused by:
questions.why: Light stroking contracts precapillary sphincters, draining the capillaries and producing pallor for ~15 s.

questions.stem: Fetal haemoglobin binds oxygen more avidly than adult haemoglobin because it has a:
questions.why: HbF binds 2,3-DPG poorly, so its oxygen affinity is higher than maternal HbA, favouring placental O2 uptake.

questions.stem: Fetal haemoglobin is normally largely replaced by adult haemoglobin by about:
questions.why: HbF usually disappears by around 4 months after birth as HbA predominates.
